title: sleep
hook: a stool stands on three legs; the Charaka Samhita says a life does too, and one of them is sleep

segments.voice: Last week ended with food as practice, and the Chandogya's chain: pure intake, a clear inner being, every knot loosened. Did you take one thing in slowly, on purpose? Day one thousand three hundred fourteen.

A milking stool has three legs, and there's a reason. On a rough barn floor, three legs always find their footing. Pull one away, though, and the whole thing tips. The Charaka Samhita, one of Ayurveda's classical texts, describes a human life the same way, propped up by three supports. We've just spent our days on the first of them, food. The second is easily treated as the empty space between the parts of the day that count. Today we start on sleep.
screen: `A STOOL ON THREE LEGS.` → `PULL ONE, IT TIPS.` → `THE SECOND SUPPORT.`

segments.voice: Charaka's word is upastambha, a support or prop, the kind that keeps something standing. He names three for life. Food. Sleep. And brahmacharya, which here means a disciplined, restrained way of living, especially around desire. Held well, he says, these three keep a body endowed with strength, good color and growth. Then, in a later chapter, he makes a large claim about sleep. In paraphrase: happiness and unhappiness, strength and weakness, knowing and not knowing, even life itself, depend on sleep, on whether it's taken rightly or wrongly. That's a lot to hang on something done with the eyes closed. Three things follow. First, sleep isn't time off from the practice. In this picture it's one of the legs the practice stands on. A morning routine, a careful meal, a quiet sit: all of them lean on the night before. Second, Charaka puts happiness and knowing on the list, not just the body. Sleep, here, reaches into the mind as well as the body. Third, rightly or wrongly. The text doesn't praise sleep as such. It talks about sleep in the right measure and at the right time, and it warns that too much, too little or at the wrong hour does harm. One more thing, said plainly. The classical texts offer a way of noticing, not a diagnosis. Sleep trouble that lasts, or snoring that stops and starts, or exhaustion that won't lift: those go to a doctor. What Charaka adds to an ordinary evening is a change of rank. Sleep stops being leftover time, and becomes a support.
screen: `UPASTAMBHA: A SUPPORT` · `FOOD, SLEEP, A DISCIPLINED LIFE` · `HAPPINESS AND KNOWING HANG ON IT` · `RIGHT MEASURE, RIGHT TIME`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: let something hold you. Sit or lie down, wherever you are. Notice what's under you: a chair, a floor, a bed. Let the weight go down into it, a little more with each breath out. Shoulders, then arms, then hands. The back. The legs, all the way to the heels. Nothing to fall asleep to, nothing to achieve. Just the feeling of being propped up by something that isn't you. If you pray, you can give thanks for the last night of rest you had. The bell holds the time.
Sleep. Nidra, in Sanskrit. For Charaka, one of three supports of life, with food and a disciplined way of living. Today's word.
Your line: sleep. Tonight, treat going to bed as part of the day instead of the end of it: choose the time on purpose, and keep it. Day one thousand three hundred fourteen.

howItsDone: In Ayurveda's classical routine, sleep at a regular hour belongs to the round of the day and night, and the texts count it among the three supports of life.

notes: First day of the sleep block. Confirm the three upastambhas at Sutrasthana 11.35 (Charaka uses svapna/nidra for sleep) and the gloss of brahmacharya as 'a disciplined, restrained way of living, especially around desire'.
Sutrasthana 21 (verse numbers approximate, around 21.36): the list of things that depend on sleep. The lesson softens 'life and death' to 'even life itself'; confirm.
'Steady, strong and bright' is a loose paraphrase of Charaka's benefits of the three supports (strength, complexion, growth); confirm.
Science-seat line: lasting sleep trouble, interrupted snoring, unexplained exhaustion go to a doctor. The 'short night and a short temper' line is an everyday picture, not a claim from the text.

Editor pass: removed 'most of us' and the 'short night, short temper often' claim; Sutrasthana 21 is not wholly about sleep, so 'a chapter given over to sleep' became 'a later chapter'; benefits now paraphrase 11.35 (strength, color, growth); cut the stock 'stops a reader' and the 'plain word' line repeated from day 1312; varied the lead-in.
The milking-stool hook is an analogy, not a claim about the text.
